p1.title: Passage 1
paras: A map that showed every pebble and blade of grass would be as large as the country it described, and therefore useless. Its value lies precisely in what it leaves out. Scientific models share this character. An economist's model of a market, a climatologist's model of the atmosphere, or a physicist's picture of a gas as countless tiny colliding balls all simplify the world deliberately, ignoring features judged irrelevant to the question at hand. The model of a gas as bouncing balls is false in many respects, yet it predicts how pressure changes with temperature remarkably well.

The danger arises when the simplification is forgotten. A model built to answer one question may be pressed into service for another for which its omissions are crucial, and its users, impressed by its past successes, may mistake the map for the territory. Many failures of forecasting, in economics especially, have been traced not to bad mathematics but to assumptions that were reasonable in ordinary times and disastrous in unusual ones. The remedy is not to abandon models, without which no complex system could be studied at all, but to use them with an awareness of their boundaries. A good scientist asks not only what a model predicts, but what it was designed to ignore.

p2.title: Passage 2
paras: In many towns, the most prominent buildings near the railway station are not temples or offices but coaching institutes, their hoardings displaying the photographs of students who secured top ranks in competitive examinations. Lakhs of adolescents leave home each year to spend two or three years preparing for a single entrance test, often at considerable cost to families who borrow to pay the fees. The examinations themselves are designed to rank vast numbers of candidates for a small number of seats, and they reward speed, pattern recognition and relentless practice. Coaching institutes have become extraordinarily efficient at supplying exactly these qualities.

The cost of this efficiency is borne in ways that rank lists do not record. Schooling in the final years becomes a formality, attended for the certificate while real study happens elsewhere. Curiosity that does not serve the syllabus is treated as a distraction. For the many who do not succeed, the experience can leave a lasting sense of failure at the age of seventeen, sometimes with tragic consequences. It would be unfair to blame students or even the institutes, which respond rationally to the incentives before them. The root lies in a scarcity of good institutions of higher learning and in an examination system that asks one test to bear the weight of a young person's future. Until those change, the coaching industry will continue to flourish.

questions.q: Which title best suits the passage?
opts: How to Draw an Accurate Map
questions.why: Main idea: models, like maps, are useful because they simplify, but their limits must be remembered.

questions.q: The model of a gas as bouncing balls is mentioned as an example of a model that:
opts: Is false in many respects yet predicts well.
questions.why: Detail: it 'is false in many respects, yet it predicts how pressure changes with temperature remarkably well'.

questions.q: To "mistake the map for the territory" means to:
opts: Draw a map larger than the country it shows.
Treat a simplified representation as if it were reality itself.
questions.why: Inference: users 'impressed by its past successes' forget 'the simplification'.

questions.q: According to the passage, many failures of economic forecasting have been traced to:
opts: Assumptions that suited ordinary times but failed in unusual ones.
questions.why: Detail: 'not to bad mathematics but to assumptions that were reasonable in ordinary times and disastrous in unusual ones'.

questions.q: The author's attitude towards scientific models is best described as:
opts: Indifferent to how they are used.
Appreciative of their usefulness but alert to their limits.
Contemptuous, since all models are false.
questions.why: Tone: 'The remedy is not to abandon models... but to use them with an awareness of their boundaries'.

questions.q: Which of the following best states the main idea of the passage?
opts: Entrance examinations accurately measure a student's curiosity.
Students who fail entrance tests lack effort.
The coaching boom is a rational response to scarce seats and high-stakes tests, but it carries serious hidden costs.
Coaching institutes are the root cause of problems in education.
questions.why: Main idea: institutes 'respond rationally to the incentives', but there is a 'cost of this efficiency', and 'The root lies in a scarcity of good institutions'.

questions.q: According to the passage, entrance examinations reward:
opts: speed, pattern recognition and relentless practice.
questions.why: Detail: 'they reward speed, pattern recognition and relentless practice'.

questions.q: Which reform would the author most likely support?
opts: Basing admission on several assessments rather than a single test.
Reducing the number of seats in colleges.
questions.why: Inference: the author blames 'an examination system that asks one test to bear the weight of a young person's future' and says it is unfair to blame the institutes.

questions.q: The author's attitude towards coaching institutes is that they:
opts: are wholly responsible for students' distress.
should not be blamed, since they respond rationally to existing incentives.
are of no importance to the discussion.
provide the ideal model of education.
questions.why: Tone: 'It would be unfair to blame students or even the institutes, which respond rationally to the incentives before them.'

questions.q: As used in the passage, 'relentless' means:
questions.why: Vocabulary: 'relentless practice' is practice that never lets up.
